news.title: That Antivirus Renewal Email Is Fake — Check Your Bank Statement First
news.excerpt: Scammers are emailing people a convincing receipt that says their antivirus subscription just auto-renewed for about $130, with a handy link to cancel it. There is no subscription and no charge. The cancel page is a fake form that collects your name, email address and number so a fake support agent can call you next. Don't click the link and don't fill in that form. Check your own bank statement instead — no charge means nothing to cancel.

news.title: Scammers Fooled a Bank Into Handing Over 50,000 Customers' Private Files
news.excerpt: Scammers just fooled the online bank Revolut into handing over private files for about 50,000 customers — birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, copies of passports and driver's licenses, even the selfies taken to verify accounts. How? They posed as a government agency using a real government email address, so the request looked completely legitimate. Expect very convincing follow-up scams that quote your real details. Don't trust caller ID or an official-looking email: hang up and call the company back at the number on your card or statement.

news.title: Fake Deal Sites Surge After Apple's iPhone Launch — How to Pay Smart
news.excerpt: Looking for a deal on a hot new gadget? The Guardian warned Sunday about fake shopping sites built to cash in on Apple's new iPhone launch — researchers watched more than 200 copycat websites appear in a single day. They look convincing, and they often insist on payment by bank transfer or digital currency, skipping the protection your card gives you. Buy only from stores you know, pay by credit card, and treat a too-good price as a warning sign. Already paid? Call your bank right away.

news.title: Scammers Can Fake Your Grandchild's Voice Now — Here's the Family Fix
news.excerpt: Scammers are calling grandparents in a voice that sounds exactly like their grandchild — because a computer cloned it. The Better Business Bureau warned families this week, just before Grandparents' Day: crooks lift a few seconds of audio and family details from social media, then fake a crash or an arrest and beg for money fast. Hang up and call your grandchild back yourself, and set up a family code word. Then lock your Facebook photos to friends-only — that's where they shop for voices.

news.title: Scammers Posing as Microsoft Support Are After Your Password — Hang Up
news.excerpt: Microsoft issued a warning Friday: crooks are calling people while pretending to be the computer's support team — sometimes claiming to be Microsoft — saying your account needs an urgent "security update." Then they text you a link to a sign-in page that looks exactly like the real one. Real Microsoft never calls first. Hang up, delete the text, and if you already typed your password, change it now — then call me.

posts.title: Is your Windows 11 computer about to stop getting free security updates? Microsoft's October 13 deadline takes 30 seconds to check in Settings
posts.summary: On October 13, Microsoft stops sending free security updates to the older version of Windows 11 that shipped back in 2024. The fix is free and it's just an update: open Settings > Windows Update, click Check for updates, and install everything it offers — your files and programs stay exactly where they are. Not sure which version you have? Press the Start button and type About your PC; it's written right there in plain text.
posts.truth: Updates feel like nagging, so people put them off — and then they get used to the nagging. Most people don't realize that once a version of Windows stops getting updates, every new flaw the bad guys find from that day forward stays open forever. Nothing warns you. One morning the computer is simply easier to break into than it was the day before. The honest answer is that the newest free version of Windows 11 is the safest one, and getting it costs you one evening at home with a cup of coffee and a progress bar.

posts.title: Before you give up on that slow old laptop, look it up on iFixit — free step-by-step guides at ifixit.com
posts.summary: iFixit is a free website — ifixit.com — with thousands of step-by-step guides and pictures for bringing laptops and desktops back to life. Look up your machine, see what the job takes, and decide whether it's a 20-minute afternoon job or one for the shop. Parts and small toolkits are sold there too.
posts.truth: Most people don't realize how much of a computer can be brought back from the dead — a worn-out battery, a clogged fan, a dying drive, all fixable. The companies that build these machines would rather you never learned that, because a replacement sale beats a repair every time. iFixit is the free counterweight: a repair manual the manufacturers never gave you, with real photos and honest difficulty ratings. The honest answer is even if you never turn a single screw yourself, ten minutes on iFixit turns you into an informed customer — you'll know whether you're being quoted a fair job or a fairy tale.

posts.title: Your inkjet printer dried up again? A Brother laser printer prints on the first try even after months of sitting — Wirecutter's 2026 home-office pick starts around $210 at brother-usa.com
posts.summary: Laser printers use toner powder, not liquid ink, so there's nothing to dry out and clog. Wirecutter's 2026 pick for the best home-office laser printer is a Brother — about $210 at brother-usa.com, Best Buy, or Amazon — and a black toner cartridge lasts thousands of pages.
posts.truth: I see this all the time: somebody buys a cheap inkjet, prints two pages a month, and every month the ink dries a little more until the thing refuses to print the morning they need a boarding pass or a tax form. Then they buy new cartridges that cost half what the printer did. The honest answer is the cheap printer is the most expensive one in the room. A laser printer costs more up front and almost nothing after that — the powder never dries out, even if the printer sits all summer. Most people don't realize a single black toner cartridge can outlast a stack of ink cartridges that cost twice as much. If you would rather buy than keep nursing ink cartridges, Wirecutter's pick runs about $210 at brother-usa.com, Best Buy, or Amazon.

posts.title: Your LG TV reports what you watch to advertisers — turn it off free in Settings > General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus
posts.summary: A new investigation put it back in the news this week: LG smart TVs record a fingerprint of everything you watch — cable, streaming, even over-the-air — and send it home so advertisers can target you. The fix is one free switch, no account needed: press the Settings (gear) button on the remote, go to General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus, and turn it off. On Samsung TVs the similar switch lives under Settings > General > Terms & Privacy.
posts.truth: Here's the one that surprises everybody: the TV is a computer, and the biggest screen in the house is also the chattiest. Someone buying a television based on selling your viewing habits — what time you watch, what channel, whether it's football or the news — and you'd never know it, because it never asks twice. The honest answer is I'm not saying smash your TV; I'm saying a six-hundred-dollar TV doesn't need a second income. Two minutes with the remote and it goes back to being just a TV. The picture doesn't change one bit. You'll never miss the setting, and neither will the advertisers — they're the only ones who lose.

posts.title: Is someone in your email right now? Check your Sent folder, then open your account's recent activity page to see every device that signed in
posts.summary: Check your Sent folder for messages you never wrote, then open your email provider's recent-activity page to see every device that has signed in: for Gmail it's myaccount.google.com/security, for Outlook or Hotmail it's account.microsoft.com/security. Anything you don't recognize means it's time to change your password — or come see me.
posts.truth: Here's the trick I wish every customer knew: when crooks break into an email, they don't leave a note — but they do leave footprints. Almost every email account keeps a list of every device that signed in, where it was, and when, and almost nobody ever looks at it. The honest answer is the "weird thing" people notice — friends saying you sent them a strange link, a password reset email they never asked for — is usually the third or fourth clue, not the first. Two minutes in that activity list and you'll know for sure. Most of the time it's just you, your phone, and your tablet, and you'll sleep better.

posts.title: Columbia County's library pays for Career Online High School — a free, accredited high school diploma you finish from your kitchen table
posts.summary: Call the Columbia County Public Library at (386) 758-2111 and ask about Career Online High School. It's a real, accredited high school diploma plus a career certificate, done entirely online at your own pace, and the grant pays the whole cost — you don't pay a dime. The library has a page with the enrollment steps on columbiacountyfla.com (search "Career Online High School" on the site).
posts.truth: Most folks who never finished school assume that door closed a long time ago, and that going back means sitting in a classroom with teenagers and taking a test you won't pass. The honest answer is neither of those is true anymore. This is the same accredited diploma, from your own house, on your own hours — an hour after supper, or Sunday morning before church. The library does the paperwork and picks up the bill. I see people in this shop every week who make a good living with their hands and still feel like that missing diploma is hanging over them. It isn't too late, and it isn't expensive. It's free.

posts.title: Hard-to-read websites? Firefox's built-in Reader View turns any article into big, clear text — one click, free at firefox.com
posts.summary: Firefox is a free web browser, and its Reader View is built right in: when a website is a mess of ads and sidebars, click the page-shaped icon at the right end of the address bar and Reader View strips the page down to plain text. Click the Aa button to make the words bigger, or have the page read aloud to you. Firefox is free at firefox.com.
posts.truth: The internet used to feel like a library. Now half the time it feels like a carnival — pop-ups, videos autoplaying, three sidebars fighting over your attention. Most people don't realize the mess is the website's fault, not their eyes and not their computer, and that the cure is one click in the browser. Reader View throws all the junk out and hands you the article like a clean printed page. The honest answer is I use it every morning myself — and the read-aloud button means I can "read" the news while the coffee brews.

posts.title: Homework help for $4 a month — Khan Academy's Khanmigo is an AI tutor that explains instead of answering, at khanmigo.ai
posts.summary: Khanmigo is the AI tutor built by Khan Academy, the nonprofit that has offered free school lessons for years. It walks kids through problems step by step instead of doing the work for them. Sign up at khanmigo.ai — $4 a month for families — and the whole library of Khan Academy lessons underneath it stays free.
posts.truth: Most parents I talk to are caught between two fears: they don't want their kid copying answers off some chatbot, and they can't sit at the kitchen table re-learning seventh-grade math every night. Khanmigo was built for exactly that spot — it's the tutor that says "let's work through it together" instead of just handing over the answer, and it's run by a nonprofit, not an ad company. The honest answer is four dollars a month is less than one trip to the vending machine fund, and it buys a patient tutor that never sighs, never says "we already covered this," and is available at 9 p.m. when the worksheet is due tomorrow.

posts.title: Update Chrome, VLC, Zoom, and a dozen apps in one click — Ninite is free at ninite.com
posts.summary: Go to ninite.com, check the boxes for the free apps you already use — Chrome, Firefox, VLC, Zoom, and dozens more — and it builds you one installer. Run it once and Ninite installs or updates everything together; no toolbars, no junk offers. Keep that one file on your desktop, run it again about once a month, and every app on the list refreshes itself. Free for home use.
posts.truth: Here's the part almost nobody believes: your computer doesn't usually get broken by viruses walking in the front door — it gets broken by old programs standing in the back doorway. Criminals poke at well-known free apps that haven't been updated in a year, because the maker already published the fix and you just haven't gotten it. Updating twelve apps by hand is a Saturday morning you don't have. The honest answer is there's a website built for exactly this problem, it's been around for well over a decade, and it refuses to bundle junk — that refusal is the whole reason I trust it. One click, one download, one run, and the sneaky back doors close.

posts.title: Rapid Fiber Internet is done building — every Suwannee Valley Electric member can now get fiber internet; check your address at svec-coop.com
posts.summary: Suwannee Valley Electric's Rapid Fiber Internet finished its $93 million build this month — true fiber internet is now available to all of SVEC's members across our area. Check your address free at svec-coop.com/rapid-fiber-internet, or call SVEC at 800-447-4509 to ask when your home can connect.
posts.truth: I've heard "the internet out here is just slow" so many times that folks stopped asking why. The honest answer is it was never your computer — out in the country around Lake City, most connections travel miles of old copper lines that were never built for video calls and streaming. Rapid Fiber spent the last four years burying brand-new fiber lines past more than 28,000 homes, and they finished the job this month. If you've been paying for sluggish internet and blaming yourself, check that map. Fiber means video calls that don't freeze, movies that don't buffer, and one less thing between your family and the rest of the world.
